title: Typewriter ribbon: revive tape-automated bonding for fine-pitch memory links
idea: Inspired by the typewriter ribbon: use modern 20 um-pitch polyimide flex tape (TAB, a 1970s technology) gang-bonded to memory and processor pads, giving wide, short memory buses between separate packages without an interposer.
why: Interposer cost and capacity; wide-bus links at ~1 pJ/bit from existing flex makers.

title: Duplex printing: memory stacks on both faces of compute
idea: Like printing both sides of a page, make DUV nano-TSVs through the thinned logic die so HBM-like stacks bond to both its top and bottom faces.
why: Doubles memory shoreline and bandwidth per compute die without EUV; shorter wires cut pJ/bit.

title: CCD memory revival: bucket-brigade charge conveyors replace HBM global datalines
idea: Build buried-channel CCD lanes in the HBM core and base dies that shift whole rows of charge packets from banks to the PHY with three-phase resonant clocks, sensing only at the lane end, instead of precharging and swinging long global I/O lines.
why: Facts 5/7/8: charge packets move at ~0.1-0.2 V signal levels with recoverable clock energy, claimed 3-5x less on-die data-path energy (about half of HBM pJ/bit) and a smaller periphery.

title: Fewer, faster TSVs: serialize 16:1 inside the stack
idea: Reverse HBM's many-slow-wires rule inside the stack: each TSV carries a 16:1 serialized 25-32 Gb/s stream from compact injection-locked transceivers on each die, cutting signal TSVs from thousands to a few hundred at a relaxed 40-50 um pitch.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): TSV area and keep-out shrink ~80% and the relaxed pitch raises stack yield; costs ~0.3 pJ/bit of SerDes energy, so it suits capacity-oriented stacks rather than peak-bandwidth ones.

title: Injection-locked ring-oscillator phase stores bits inside link retimers
idea: Worsen: use leaky charge to store a bit. Flip: store each bit as the 0-or-pi phase of a sub-harmonically injection-locked CMOS ring oscillator, reviving Goto's parametron inside link retimers where clocks already run, and read it by phase comparison.
why: Capacitor-free elastic buffers built from inverters only; refresh-free while clocked. Small capacity and active power limit it to link buffering.

title: Mirrored predictors so only residuals cross the memory bus
idea: Po: memory sends guesses, not data. The HBM base die and the GPU memory controller run identical tiny value predictors (last-value, stride and delta per cacheline region) in lockstep; on each read only the entropy-coded residual against the shared prediction crosses the link.
why: Attacks 3-4 pJ/bit data-movement energy; structured tensors and pointers compress 1.5-3x, raising effective bandwidth and cutting link energy by the same factor.

title: Repurpose LCD glass-panel lines to make giant memory interposers
idea: Adapted from display makers' Gen-8 (2.2 x 2.5 m) glass TFT lines with ~1.5 um lithography: pattern copper RDL and through-glass vias at panel scale. The panels become interposers that hold dozens of memory stacks around accelerators.
why: Silicon interposers are reticle-limited and capacity-bound; panels amortize over ~70x a 300 mm wafer's area, cutting interposer cost per area ~5-10x and freeing CoWoS capacity.

title: Bipolar-battery voltage stacking of HBM core dies
idea: Bipolar battery stacks put cells in series so the same current flows straight through every cell. Do this with four groups of HBM core dies across a ~4.4 V rail: each group sees ~1.1 V and the same current is reused in every tier. Small switched-capacitor balancers on the base die absorb load mismatch between tiers.
why: Cuts supply current, and with it the count of power TSVs/bumps and PDN IR loss, by about 4x. That shrinks HBM's TSV tax and could return 10-15% of die area or allow taller stacks.

title: Electric-eel series stack: voltage-stacked HBM tiers
idea: An electric eel sums voltage by stacking thousands of electrocytes in series. Likewise HBM tiers are wired in electrical series: the package supplies ~8-12 V, the same current passes down through each tier at ~1.1 V each, and small on-die push-pull regulators balance the tiers. Supply current, and with it the power TSV count and IR drop, falls about N-fold.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6) and power delivery: power TSVs and bumps fall ~8x for an 8-high stack, freeing area, raising yield and cutting package I^2R loss.

title: Top-k memory: base die filters KV cache before the link
idea: Invert 'memory returns what was asked for': for attention, the host sends the query vector to the HBM base die, which scores keys in low precision across the KV pages beneath it and returns only the top-k keys/values at full precision.
why: Long-context decode is KV-bandwidth-bound; returning 5-10% of KV entries cuts link traffic 10-20x and lets longer contexts live in fewer, cheaper stacks.

title: Thick-copper superhighway layer for low-swing bank-to-PHY transport
idea: Po: wires thicker than transistors are tall. One added mask lays a 10-20 um thick copper top layer that carries global data from far banks to the I/O with very low resistance, so data can move at 100-200 mV swing.
why: Cuts on-die data movement energy (a large part of the 5.9 pJ per useful bit) ~2x without new transistors.

title: Harvest-and-rebin HBM from retired accelerators
idea: MAGNIFY HBM's useful life: base dies carry standard re-ball pads and a full built-in self-test, so stacks pulled from retired GPUs are retested, graded and rebonded into CXL memory expanders.
why: Scarce-resource and capital intensity: second-life memory adds supply without wafers; claims 10-20% extra effective bits per year.

title: Backside-powered base die frees the whole front for signals
idea: Invert 'power and signals share the same face': build the HBM base die on a U.S. backside-power process (Intel 18A PowerVia, Arizona) so power enters from the back and every front-side bond carries data.
why: Signal bond density roughly doubles, ~2x I/O per base die, with cleaner power delivery for faster stacks.

title: Refresh-free cells let memory sit directly on hot logic
idea: Worsen: never stack memory on logic because heat wrecks DRAM retention. Flip: since SRAM and ROM hold state at 105 C+ without refresh, bond them directly on the hottest compute tiles with a copper thermal-pillar grid through the memory, and push any DRAM to the cooler package edge.
why: Data movement: the nearest memory tier sits at ~0 mm, and the thermal budget no longer couples to retention or refresh.

title: Magnetostriction: magnetoelectric nano-antennas give chiplet memory links without interposer wires
idea: FeGaB/AlN magnetoelectric antennas radiate at their GHz acoustic resonance rather than their electromagnetic wavelength, making them ~100x smaller than patch antennas; arrays on memory and compute chiplets talk wirelessly through mold compound with no interposer routing.
why: Removes silicon interposer (CoWoS capacity and cost) for low-to-mid bandwidth memory chiplets; packaging capex down; ~1-3 pJ/bit target.

title: Age-out tiering: base die evicts rows before retention, never refreshes
idea: Ideal: every row is either fresh or gone. Closest achievable: the HBM base die keeps a per-row age counter; rows nearing ~50 ms without natural access are compressed and written once to a dense non-volatile tier (stacked NAND or a remote pool) and the DRAM row is freed, making DRAM a pure write-back cache of recent data with no REF command.
why: Fact 3: refresh power goes to zero and idle DRAM can be fully powered off; long-lived cold data costs one write instead of ~16 refreshes per second forever.

title: Circulating drum memory: streaming access refreshes ultra-leaky cheap cells
idea: Capacitor size and leakage specs exist only to hold charge for 64 ms; if every row is read-and-restored every 100 us because data circulates through compute like a drum, retention can be 640x worse. That permits planar MIM capacitors on short bitlines and leaky access devices in fully depreciated 28-40 nm fabs, with no high-AR etch and no EUV, behind a controller that streams rows in fixed order.
why: Strips capital (~55% of wafer cost) and the capacitor/EUV steps; claimed 10-100x lower cost per GB with high uncertainty; trades random access for sequential revolution latency.

title: Magnetic dipole chaining: field-aligned nickel-particle printed films for fine-pitch z-interconnect
idea: Print a curable polymer loaded with nickel microparticles on R2R film; an applied magnetic field chains the particles into vertical columns at ~5 um pitch before UV cure, giving an anisotropic z-conductor that attaches memory dies to printed interposers without bumps.
why: Packaging cost and pitch (fact 6): bumpless, solderless die attach on R2R lines at 5-10x finer pitch than conventional ACF.

title: Prior counteraction: pre-emphasis lets HBM-class links run on organic substrate
idea: TRIZ #9 Preliminary anti-action: put feed-forward equalization and per-lane deskew in a 28 nm base/hub die that pre-distorts signals against the known channel loss. This allows 1024-bit memory links on ordinary 2/2 um organic fan-out substrates instead of silicon interposers. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Capital and the CoWoS chokepoint: no silicon interposer for HBM-class memory, ~30-50% lower packaging cost and existing OSAT capacity, at ~1 pJ/bit.

title: Progressive-JPEG bit-plane memory: fetch only needed precision
idea: Satellite and web imagery stream progressive bit planes so receivers stop when good enough. Store tensors bit-plane-sliced across columns (sign/exponent plane first, then mantissa planes); each read requests only the top N planes and only those columns are sensed and sent.
why: Most inference reads need 2-4 effective bits of a 16-bit value; energy per access scales with planes fetched, ~4-8x lower, ~10x with shared block exponents.

title: Utility lineman's high-voltage lines: 12 V delivery into the stack
idea: Linemen send power at high voltage to cut current: deliver 12 V up a few power TSVs and convert to ~1 V with switched-capacitor converters in the memory base die, cutting the current per power via about 10x.
why: Electromigration scales with current density and degrades steeply at 125 C, so 10x less current lets power-TSV count drop about 70%, freeing area for signals and memory.

title: Magnetic stray-field vias couple stacked MRAM dies
idea: Eliminate TSVs in a non-volatile stack: each die carries 'transmitter' nanomagnet columns switched by spin-orbit torque, and the die above senses their stray field with TMR sensors across a thinned-die/bond gap of a few um; the vertical link itself holds state with zero power.
why: Removes TSV area tax and via reveal; vertical signalling at ~fJ switching energy. Field decays steeply over microns, so this is a long shot.

title: Ni: electroless-nickel sidewall wiring replaces TSVs in die stacks
idea: Route HBM core-die I/O to the die edge, stack the dies, then laser-pattern and electrolessly plate Ni/Cu/Au traces down the polished stack sidewall at ~10 um pitch (~4,000 lines on a 10 mm die perimeter) to the base die, which keeps the standard HBM PHY.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): core dies need no TSVs, keep-outs or backside processing, saving ~5-10% die area and improving stack yield.

title: Wavelength-addressed banks: the address is the light colour
idea: Box: 1T1C sub-arrays x wordline fired by a ring-filter photodiode x bitline read by microring modulator x WDM bus x SiN waveguides deposited below 400 C on DRAM BEOL x back-end photonics. Each bank owns one wavelength; a request is a pulse at that colour that only its filter absorbs, firing the wordline with no global row/column decoder tree, and data returns on a modulated carrier.
why: Periphery (fact 7) and data movement (fact 5): removes much of the global decode and long electrical I/O; speculative ~30% die-area saving and <1 pJ/bit off-die.

title: Full-row dump to a base-die SRAM row cache
idea: MAGNIFY transfer size to an entire 8 KB row: on activation, the row crosses an 8K-bit hybrid-bonded bus into a base-die SRAM row cache, the DRAM row closes at once, and random sub-reads are served from SRAM.
why: 128x overfetch and row hammer: the activated row is used fully and opened only once; claims ~3x less energy per useful bit.

title: Coin-struck dual damascene: via and trench in one press
idea: Make a nanoimprint stamp with two relief heights, like a coin die, so one press forms both the via and the trench of an interposer wiring level in resist. One etch and fill then replaces two litho and two etch passes.
why: Halves the BEOL step count and mask count for interposer and base-die RDL, cutting capital per interconnect layer.

title: Diamond interleaf wafers make DRAM-on-logic thermally survivable
idea: The shortest data path is DRAM directly on logic, but heat raises leakage and refresh rate. Bond 30 um polycrystalline CVD diamond wafers (k ~1500 W/mK) between logic and DRAM tiers with laser-drilled Cu vias, spreading hotspots sideways before they reach the cells.
why: Lets DRAM sit ~50 um from compute (~0.1 pJ/bit vs 3-4) while holding cells <=85 C so refresh does not double (facts 5, 3).

title: Vertical product codes striped through the stack's TSV columns
idea: Rotate part of the codeword 90 degrees: each die keeps a horizontal row code for its 1% cell errors, and a vertical Reed-Solomon code places one symbol per die along the same TSV column, so a dead TSV or an entire failed die becomes a correctable erasure in the same structure.
why: Raises HBM stack yield (fact 6, -20-30%) toward ~95% while tolerating 1% cell BER and removing redundancy rows and repair fuses from periphery (fact 7).

title: Child's 'mom keeps the flashlight': remote lasers outside the hot zone
idea: Lasers wear out fast at 125 C, so keep them where it is cool: a remote laser bank in a 50 C zone sends CW light over glass fibre, and the 125 C memory package holds only athermal SiN-assisted Mach-Zehnder modulators and Ge detectors, with no light source inside.
why: Allows optical memory links (~1 pJ/bit, cm-to-m reach) in 125 C automotive and industrial packages, so the packages can use remote DRAM instead of soldered-down hot LPDDR.

title: Vacuum-annulus TSV liners cut via capacitance threefold
idea: TSV capacitance (~30-50 fF) is set by liner permittivity: C ~ 2*pi*eps*L/ln(r2/r1). Deposit a sacrificial carbon liner, fill Cu, then ash the carbon through vent slots to leave a sealed ~200 nm vacuum annulus (k=1) around each via, which also mechanically decouples copper expansion from silicon.
why: ~3x lower TSV CV^2 and crosstalk in HBM stacks, and the stress-free gap shrinks keep-out zones, cutting TSV area tax ~20-30% (fact 6).

title: Contactless memory slot: PCB coil pairs replace DIMM connector pins
idea: Substitute metal edge-finger contacts with arrays of near-field coupled coil pairs etched in ordinary PCB copper on module and motherboard, driven by a small transceiver FPGA/ASIC; modules slide in without contact, are hot-swappable and the slot pitch can shrink.
why: Data movement and capacity: no connector stubs or wear, denser slots per channel, ~2x modules per board area.

title: Stochastic resonance: noise-assisted bistable receivers detect 30 mV memory signals
idea: Drive an array of bistable comparators with deliberately injected uncorrelated noise so a sub-threshold 30 mV signal biases their switching statistics; majority-summing 16 comparators recovers each bit at low BER on a fraction of today's swing.
why: I/O CV^2 energy (facts 5, 10): ~100x lower swing energy minus comparator overhead, net ~3-5x pJ/bit on short interposer links.

title: Xerography revival: electrophotographic copper-toner printing of package wiring
idea: Revive Carlson's 1938 xerography: a laser-imaged photoconductor drum picks up charged copper-nanoparticle toner and transfers it to the package substrate, followed by sintering and electroless copper thickening, giving maskless, resist-free 10-20 um RDL.
why: Constraint: no photoresist at all, so no PFAS PAGs or fluorosurfactants; a printer-class tool (~$1M) replaces lithography for package redistribution, cutting capital and enabling distributed US packaging.

title: Asymmetry: read-mostly weight tier on legacy NAND with wide parallel reads
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: model weights are written once and read billions of times, so store them in a tier built on 64-layer-era NAND lines. A 28 nm controller reads thousands of planes in parallel, streaming each layer ahead into a small DRAM staging buffer to hide ~30 us read latency, while writes stay slow and rare. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Do DRAM's job with less DRAM: moving weights out of HBM/DRAM frees 30-70% of memory for KV cache, at NAND cost per bit (~1/10 of DRAM) from depreciated lines.

title: Trilogy's wafer-scale dream fixed: an unsawn DRAM wafer as memory backplane
idea: Gene Amdahl's Trilogy failed on wafer-scale yield and on CTE-driven delamination between the wafer and its packaging. Keep a whole 300 mm DRAM wafer unsawn (~3-4 TB raw at ~0.4 Gb/mm2), map out bad reticles at test, and hybrid-bond logic chiplets face-to-face only onto good reticle sites; because everything is silicon on silicon there is no CTE mismatch, and dicing, packaging, TSVs and interposers disappear.
why: Removes package, TSV and interposer cost (fact 6) and data-movement energy (~0.05 pJ/bit face-to-face): TB-class memory at on-die bandwidth, with a claimed 30-50% lower cost per delivered GB than HBM.

title: Address-event storage keeps only coordinates of nonzero values
idea: When activations are >99% zero (ReLU-fied LLMs, spiking nets, event sensors), storing the zeros wastes ~99% of bits. Store tensors as address-event streams (index plus small value) in the interface die, expand them only inside SRAM next to the MAC arrays, and train with sparsity regularizers targeting 99%+.
why: Bytes stored and moved fall 30-100x for sparse tensors; trades model architecture freedom.

title: Cellphone LTCC radio modules become 30-layer ceramic memory substrates
idea: Adapted from the low-temperature co-fired ceramic tape lines of 1990s handset RF front-ends: silver wiring is screen-printed on 30+ green tape layers with punched vias and co-fired, then DRAM dies are flip-chipped around a processor. Dense routing comes with no silicon interposer and no lithography below 50 um.
why: Interposer cost and the CoWoS bottleneck: tape-casting and screen-printing tools are cheap and U.S.-buildable; 50 um lines support 512-1024-bit wide-slow buses per die at a fraction of interposer cost.

title: Wire-in-resin printed packages stack commodity memory BGAs
idea: Substitute substrate layers and TSVs with a printer-robot that embeds insulated fine copper wire inside 3D-printed resin frames as it prints, routing 3D connections between stacked commodity LPDDR packages and the host board.
why: Capital and density: dense memory modules without new silicon or substrate fabs; prototypes in days by a small team.

title: Sheet-cake cut-anywhere memory sea bonded to logic wafers
idea: Bond whole DRAM wafers made of identical repeating tiles onto logic wafers, then choose product capacity at the dicing saw like cutting sheet cake. Tile-to-tile links are stitched so any rectangle works.
why: Wafer-on-wafer bonding cuts assembly cost; cut-anywhere sizing removes SKU-mismatch inventory and stranded supply.

title: 77 K liquid-nitrogen memory packages with minute-long retention
idea: Worsen: run DRAM hot so leakage forces 32-64 ms refresh. Flip: immerse memory packages and interposers in liquid nitrogen, where junction leakage falls by orders of magnitude (retention of minutes) and copper resistance drops ~6x, so refresh nearly vanishes and long links get cheaper.
why: Refresh (fact 3) and data movement: refresh power near zero, lower wire energy; LN2 is made from air anywhere, unlike scarce helium.

title: Coral accretion: mask-free additively grown ceramic memory interposer
idea: Corals build a skeleton by accreting mineral layer by layer. A ceramic interposer is grown the same way, alternating aerosol-jet-printed alumina-glass dielectric with nano-silver traces densified by cold sintering below 200 C, so each package's routing prints straight from CAD with no masks and no wafer fab.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: interposers from small U.S. shops with $1-3M printers instead of $B fabs; adequate for 20-40 um-pitch CXL memory expanders and chiplet modules.

title: Two-phase immersion memory bricks drop DIMM spacing to millimetres
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Mount dies on 0.2 mm boards at 1.5 mm pitch with boiling-channel gaps and submerge them in dielectric fluid; nucleate boiling removes ~100 W/cm2, so heat spreaders and airflow spacing disappear.
why: Volumetric density: air-cooled DIMM pitch is ~10 mm; 1.5 mm pitch gives ~6-10x bits per liter while dropping spreaders and fans offsets the fluid cost.

title: Bitline-direct bonding: one bond per 16 bitlines
idea: MAGNIFY interface width down to the subarray: hybrid-bond each subarray's local I/O lines (one 1 um pad per 16 bitlines) straight to compute-die pads, deleting global I/O lines, column muxes, the DDR PHY and most of the DRAM periphery.
why: Periphery (~49% of die) and data-movement energy; claims ~30-40% more bits per DRAM wafer and <0.1 pJ/bit transfers.

title: Diamond fly-cut planarization enables CMP-free hybrid bonding
idea: Box: DRAM x standard x standard x Cu-Cu surface-activated bonding x Si x single-point diamond fly-cutting plus Ar fast-atom-beam activation in vacuum. Bond surfaces are flattened by dry ultra-precision fly-cutting and activated in UHV, eliminating CMP slurry, post-CMP scrubbing and DI rinses.
why: Water: CMP and post-CMP cleans are among the largest UPW users in hybrid bonding; the dry route cuts >10x and removes slurry chemistry supply.

title: Photophone revival: infrared micro-LEDs signal straight through thinned silicon stacks
idea: Like Bell's 1880 photophone sending speech on light, place 1.3-1.55 um InGaAs micro-LEDs on one die and Ge photodiodes on dies above; silicon is transparent at these wavelengths, so data crosses several thinned dies vertically with no via.
why: Constraint: no TSV etch and no fluorinated plasma or cleans; hundreds of vertical channels per stack at ~1 pJ/bit decouple stack bandwidth from TSV yield (fact 6).

title: Spatial pipelining: activations ride chip-to-chip links, never parking
idea: Ideal: data is always moving and never at rest, so nothing has to be retained. Closest achievable: map a model layer-per-chiplet across a wafer or board so activations stream over short die-to-die links from one tile's SRAM buffer to the next, with weights pinned in each tile's local static storage and no DRAM holding activations.
why: Zero refresh power and fact 5: ~0.1 pJ/bit per hop vs 3-4 pJ/bit for an HBM round trip; DRAM demand for activations falls to zero.

title: Search-engine Bloom filter skips DRAM row activations
idea: Web search engines consult tiny Bloom filters before touching shards. Keep compact locality-sensitive-hash signatures of KV pages and embedding rows in logic-side SRAM; the controller activates a DRAM row only when its signature predicts relevance, so most rows are never opened.
why: Row activation is a third or more of access energy; skipping ~90% of activations in retrieval, attention and recsys gives ~10x lower energy per useful access with no memory-side change.

title: Equipotentiality: constant-voltage current-mode TSV signaling
idea: TRIZ #12 Equipotentiality (avoid raising and lowering): a low-impedance common-gate receiver holds each TSV at a fixed mid-rail voltage, and data is sent as the direction of a ~50 uA current. The TSV and microbump capacitance never charges or discharges.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and voltage floor (fact 10): IO energy no longer scales with CV^2, for ~3-5x lower pJ/bit on capacitive vertical links.

title: Kintsugi artist: liquid-metal microcapsules that heal cracked bonds
idea: Kintsugi fills cracks with gold: embed microcapsules of gallium-indium alloy, with a barrier shell, around microbump fields; when a fatigue crack forms, the capsules break and liquid metal wicks into the gap to restore conduction.
why: Self-repairs interconnect opens during 10 years at 125 C, which extends package life without big redundancy; risky because gallium embrittles Al and Cu.

title: Optane Memory Mode fixed: set-associative DRAM cache with on-controller tags
idea: Optane's Memory Mode used a direct-mapped DRAM near-memory cache, and its conflict misses made performance unpredictable, which killed adoption. Put a 16-way set-associative tag array (SRAM, ~1/512 of capacity) and a way predictor in the CXL memory controller, so a DRAM slice of 1/8 capacity fronts a cheap dense tier (NAND-backed, LPDDR or retired DDR4) with predictable miss rates under 5%.
why: Do DRAM's job with less: cuts DRAM bits per server 4-8x for capacity-bound workloads while keeping ~90-95% of all-DRAM performance, directly offsetting the 4x price spike.

title: Universality: coaxial TSV acting as signal, decap and heat pipe
idea: TRIZ #6 Universality: build each signal TSV as a coax with a Cu core, a 20 nm high-k ZrO2 liner and a grounded Cu sleeve. The shielded core carries data at tight pitch, the sleeve-to-substrate stack acts as distributed decoupling capacitance, and the extra copper conducts heat up the stack.
why: HBM TSV tax and power integrity (fact 6): 2x tighter TSV pitch without crosstalk, and no separate decap or dummy thermal TSVs, for a ~20-30% smaller TSV region.

title: MCM known-good-die curse fixed: contactless near-field wafer test
idea: 1990s multichip modules died of the known-good-die problem, and HBM repeats it because hybrid-bond pads cannot be touched by probe needles (scratches ruin bonding), so dies are bonded half-tested. Add a field of tiny capacitive/inductive near-field couplers in top metal and test each DRAM wafer at full speed, including burn-in and retention, through a matching contactless probe card before any bonding.
why: HBM stack yield (fact 6) and capital: full at-speed known-good-die screening could recover most of the 20-30% stack loss and the scrapped base dies, for <0.5% die area.

title: Myelinated interposer links with nodes-of-Ranvier regenerators
idea: Long GPU-to-memory interposer wires are cut into insulated segments wrapped in a thick low-k 'myelin' sheath, with tiny sense-and-restore 'nodes' every ~1 mm that regenerate a ~100 mV low-swing signal, as in saltatory conduction. Energy is spent only charging short low-capacitance segments, so memory stacks can sit 10-20 mm from the logic instead of 1-2 mm.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): ~2-3x lower capacitance per mm plus low swing targets <1 pJ/bit at longer reach, so more stacks can ring one accelerator beyond today's edge (shoreline) limit.

title: Firefly: burst-mode memory link wakes from off in 10 ns
idea: Like a firefly blinking: the memory PHY powers fully off between bursts and relocks in under 10 ns by keeping a forwarded clock and stored equalizer state, prototyped first on FPGA transceivers and then on a cheap MPW test chip.
why: Idle and low-utilization link power: energy per bit at 20% utilization falls 3-5x.

title: Vapor-chamber dies interleaved every eighth tier cool tall stacks
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Every eighth tier is a 50 um silicon vapor-chamber die (micro-wick etched into reclaimed wafers, water-filled, hermetically bonded) that carries heat sideways to the package edge, keeping 64-high stacks below 85 C.
why: Heat, not wiring, caps tall stacks; reclaimed-silicon cooling dies cost little, enable 10x tiers, and stop refresh rates (fact 3) from exploding.

title: Al: anodic-alumina nanowire film replaces aligned microbumps for stacking
idea: Anodize aluminum into a 20-40 um AAO membrane with ~1e10 pores/cm2, electroplate Cu into the pores, and laminate it between dies as a z-axis-only conductor: any pad overlap conducts while lateral neighbors stay isolated, so die stacking needs only coarse (+/-5 um) placement yet reaches ~2-3 um effective pitch.
why: HBM bump/TSV tax and capital (fact 6): replaces multi-$M hybrid-bond aligners and CMP-critical surfaces with a wet anodization film; ~10x microbump density at a fraction of tool cost from abundant, US-sourced Al.

title: The other way round: DRAM pushes a precompiled tensor schedule
idea: TRIZ #13 The other way round: instead of the GPU requesting every line, the compiler loads a tensor-streaming schedule into the HBM base die. The base die opens rows in a fixed order and pushes data to the accelerator, so the command/address bus becomes a rarely used control channel.
why: Data movement (fact 5), overfetch (fact 8) and row hammer (fact 9): no request traffic, no row misses, and each row opens once per pass, for ~20-30% more effective bandwidth and fewer activates.

title: Retention-dial memory: one die is both DRAM and storage
idea: Eliminate the DRAM-to-SSD copy and the two-chip BOM: use a spin-torque or ferroelectric cell whose write pulse width/amplitude sets retention (short pulse: hours, ~1e15 endurance, ns writes; long pulse: 10 years), with the base die re-writing pages in long-retention mode as they cool.
why: Removes storage-to-memory transfers and duplicate copies across tiers; in phones and edge devices one package replaces LPDDR+UFS, saving ~30% memory BOM and all load-time traffic.

title: Time-share each DRAM gigabyte among a hundred tenants via optical swap
idea: A working set only needs DRAM while it runs. Give accelerators small DRAM plus a co-packaged-optics swap path (~10 TB/s) to a NAND pool and gang-schedule jobs so each job's working set swaps in for a 10-20 ms slot; one DRAM GB serves ~100 tenants in rotation.
why: Effective DRAM per tenant ~100x lower; trades latency, job slicing and swap energy.

title: Sense-amplifier row latch reconfigured as on-die serializer
idea: Combine the bitline sense-amp row (an 8-16 kb latch already holding the opened page) with a SerDes shift register: add a segment-level pass chain so the latched row shifts directly into a local high-speed serializer next to the mat, bypassing column decoders, global I/O lines and the central datapath for streaming reads.
why: Overfetch and periphery: for streaming AI weight reads the 'overfetched' 128x row is actually used; cuts internal data-movement energy ~30-50% and column/global-I/O periphery area.

title: Magnetically chained conductive film replaces microbumps
idea: Po: the glue is the wire. Only one pad-opening mask is used; an adhesive film loaded with nickel particles is cured in a vertical magnetic field so the particles line up into columns that conduct only along z at ~5 um pitch.
why: Removes bump plating, reflow and underfill steps, lowering assembly cost and thermal stress on DRAM.

title: Zn: ZnO thin-film varistors move DRAM ESD into the package
idea: Embed ZnO multilayer varistor arrays in the DRAM package substrate under each DQ/CA ball to clamp assembly ESD, letting the die's own ESD diodes and pad structures shrink to CDM minimum while still meeting JEDEC pin capacitance and drive specs.
why: Periphery ~49% of die (fact 7): I/O and ESD rings are several % of die area and add pin capacitance; shrinking them yields ~2-4% more dies per wafer and lower I/O energy at the same interface.

title: Blessing in disguise: crosstalk-coded TSV arrays using coupling as signal
idea: TRIZ #22 Blessing in disguise: instead of shielding densely packed TSVs, group them in sets of 4-6 and send chordal vector codes (ENRZ-style). Common-mode coupling cancels while the coupled differential modes carry data, so crosstalk becomes part of the signaling.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): 2x denser TSV pitch at ~1.3-1.5 bits per wire, for ~40% less TSV area per bit.

title: Magnet-aligned nickel-chain film replaces solder microbumps
idea: Substitute microbumps with an anisotropic conductive film whose nickel microspheres are pulled into vertical columns by a permanent magnet during cure, conducting only vertically at 15-20 um pitch; a hot press and a magnet are the whole bonding line.
why: Capital and process: no bumping or reflow line, so a small team can build wide-IO memory-on-logic assemblies cheaply.

title: Tabless jelly-roll battery: rolled thin-film memory cylinder
idea: Cylindrical cells roll a long electrode sheet, and tabless designs collect current along the whole edge. Deposit IGZO gain-cell arrays (≤350 C) on a thin polyimide sheet, roll it into a jelly-roll, and bring the bus out every few mm along the edge to an end-cap logic die.
why: Gets volumetric density by rolling instead of lithographic 3D stacking, with almost no EUV or front-end capex per bit. Speculative: winding yield and bus latency are open questions.

title: Elastic buckling: roll-printed kirigami interposers pop up into 3D memory cages
idea: Print wiring on a pre-cut kirigami polyimide film; releasing pre-strain buckles it into a 3D cage that surrounds a processor with memory chiplets on all sides instead of along one edge.
why: GPU memory beachfront and interposer area (facts 5, 6): 3-4x more memory adjacency per processor from flat R2R manufacturing; thermal and mechanical robustness risk.

title: Si: unsawn wafer-scale DRAM bonded to wafer-scale compute
idea: Skip dicing: bond a whole DRAM wafer face-to-face to a whole logic wafer with reticle-stitched routing and a boot-time defect map that routes around bad DRAM dies, so die yield becomes capacity rather than scrap and no packages, interposers or TSVs exist.
why: Packaging cost and HBM tax (fact 6): ~1 TB+ per wafer pair at ~0.1 pJ/bit vertical links; a defective die just trims capacity instead of killing a stack.

title: Frequency-division memory bus: every bank owns a carrier
idea: Ideal: all banks talk at once on one wire. Closest achievable: each bank's I/O modulates its own RF carrier slot (2-40 GHz) onto a single shared interposer transmission line, and the controller demodulates all channels at once with a wideband ADC plus FFT, replacing hundreds of parallel traces.
why: Fact 6 and interposer cost: cuts trace and bump count ~16x, reducing interposer layers and area while enabling full bank-parallel access without wide buses.

title: Ferroelectric content-addressable KV store returns matches, not data
idea: Eliminate scanning KV caches over the bus: store quantized key signatures in 2-FeFET ternary CAM cells so a query is broadcast into the array and only matching token addresses come out; the index survives power cycles.
why: For sparse retrieval and long-context attention, interface traffic falls ~100x and persistent RAG indexes need no reload after power events.

title: Ga: GaN single-stage 48V-to-VDDQ regulation at the memory
idea: Mount GaN-FET hybrid switched-capacitor converters on the package substrate (and on DDR5 DIMMs in place of the 12 V PMIC) converting 48 V straight to VDD/VDDQ for the DRAM, eliminating an intermediate bus-conversion stage.
why: Energy per bit at system level: memory power delivery loses ~10-15% across two stages; single-stage GaN recovers ~5-8 points and cuts board copper, with DRAM interfaces unchanged.

title: Hearing aid: logic die reads DRAM bitlines directly through bonds
idea: Like a hearing aid amplifying faint sound: fine-pitch hybrid bonds expose DRAM local bitlines to a logic die stacked face-to-face, and the logic die's sense amplifiers resolve 50-100 mV signals directly. The DRAM-side global datapath, serializers and I/O drivers are deleted.
why: Periphery ~49% of die and I/O energy; interface energy <0.05 pJ/bit and maybe 30-40% more array area per DRAM die.

title: Nesting: DRAM dies set into pockets in the GPU backside
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting: with backside power delivery the GPU substrate is thinned anyway. Etch ~30 um pockets into its backside and set thinned DRAM dies inside, wired through nano-TSVs into the backside network, so each DRAM die sits ~30 um from the logic it feeds.
why: Data movement (fact 5): the interposer and long wires disappear, for <0.3 pJ/bit and no shoreline limit, and capacity grows with no added footprint.

title: Reel-to-reel DRAM tape wrapped around a cooling pipe
idea: Po: memory is sold by the metre. Mount bare DRAM dies on a continuous copper-on-polyimide tape (tape-automated bonding style) with fine-line flex wiring, then wrap the tape helically around a liquid-cooled tube to form a cylindrical module plugged in at one end.
why: Low-capex reel-to-reel assembly that U.S. flex-circuit makers can run, with no interposer and excellent cooling.

title: Bumpless capacitive face-to-face: the passivation is the link
idea: Reverse 'remove the dielectric to connect': leave the 0.5-1 um passivation intact, use 5 um pads on each die as coupling capacitors, and align the dies face-to-face with an adhesive; pulse-mode receivers detect the coupled edges, so no UBM, solder or CMP-grade hybrid-bond surface is needed.
why: Capital and yield: 5-10 um-pitch vertical links with only lithography and a flip-chip aligner, ~0.1 pJ/bit, and tolerance to particles that kill hybrid bonds (facts 5, 6).

title: Read-only charge-trap chiplets programmed once at wafer sort
idea: A deployed model's weights never change, and storage with no write path is the cheapest physics allows. Program 3D charge-trap arrays with weights at wafer sort via massively parallel probe cards, then ship dies with the program/erase pumps stripped, thicker retention oxide, and read-in-place sensing bonded beside compute.
why: Bit cost at or below 3D NAND (~100x+ cheaper than DRAM) with smaller periphery; trades flexibility (new model means new chips).

title: Spare tire: repurpose ECC lanes as data for hash-verified weights
idea: The 'spare tire' is the ECC chip on every server DIMM. For read-only model weights protected by per-block cryptographic hashes at load time plus periodic scrubbing, the controller uses the ECC lanes as extra data width.
why: Bandwidth and capacity: +25% on existing DIMMs, and ~11% of installed bits are reclaimed for AI weights.

title: Maskless e-beam via-ROM dies hold frozen model weights
idea: Worsen: keep read-only inference weights in refresh-hungry DRAM. Flip: make generic ROM wafers on a mature node where one via layer encodes the bits (multi-size vias for 2 bits/cell), and write that layer per model with multi-beam e-beam direct-write, so a weight die needs no capacitor, no refresh and no custom mask.
why: Refresh (fact 3) and DRAM demand: weights are often 50-80% of inference memory; 28 nm ROM at ~4F^2 is ~3-5x cheaper per bit than DRAM and needs no EUV.

title: RFID backscatter: memory die reflects and never transmits
idea: Like passive RFID tags, the memory die modulates the impedance of an RDL-patterned antenna (≤250 C) to backscatter a carrier sent by the processor. The memory side needs no transmitter or PLL.
why: Moves link power to the host side, where cooling is cheaper. Read-side energy on the memory die could drop below 0.2 pJ/bit, easing thermal limits on stacked memory.

title: Hydraulics: liquid-metal micro-well sockets for reworkable memory chiplets
idea: TRIZ #29 Pneumatics and hydraulics: replace solder microbumps with micro-wells filled with Ga-In liquid metal at ~40 um pitch on the substrate. Memory chiplets press in and are tested in place, and a failed one can be pulled out and replaced. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: HBM yield (fact 6): a bad memory chiplet no longer scraps the whole package, for ~10-20% fewer scrapped multi-thousand-dollar packages using existing OSAT tooling.

title: Elastomer micro-socket for HBM on the interposer
idea: MINIFY socket pitch to ~100 um with an anisotropic conductive elastomer, so HBM stacks are clamped (not soldered) onto the interposer and can be swapped in the field.
why: HBM yield and lifetime: a bad stack no longer scraps a ~$30k accelerator; failed stacks go back for repair and reuse.

title: Self-assembling copolymer wires quadruple interposer wiring density
idea: Po: wires draw themselves. One coarse guide mask sets trenches on the interposer, and a block-copolymer film self-assembles inside them into 4x finer lines that become copper wires after pattern transfer and plating.
why: 4x more die-to-die wires per mm of shoreline without EUV or extra masks, raising HBM channel count per GPU edge.

title: Retention-bounded FIFO DRAM die with no row decoders
idea: Ideal: a memory that is a pipe, holding data only while it flows. Closest achievable: a streaming DRAM die organized as a circular buffer of rows driven by a sequential row counter, sized so wrap-around time is below retention; it has no random row decoder, no refresh counter and only a head/tail pointer interface, serving as the staging buffer between flash or remote memory and the GPU.
why: Zero refresh by construction plus fact 7: removing decoders and refresh logic recovers ~15-20% of die area; fits weight streaming and pipeline-parallel buffers.

title: Coral reef: electroless copper grows bonds between facing pads
idea: Like coral growing into a reef: dies are held with a 2-5 um gap over the substrate, and an electroless Cu bath grows metal from both pad faces until they fuse, giving room-temperature, pressure-free interconnects. University-cleanroom feasible.
why: Capital intensity and thermal damage; no bonders or anneals, and potentially reworkable before passivation.

title: F: PTFE-laminate channels enable full-speed two-DIMMs-per-channel DDR5
idea: Route server DDR5 channels and DIMM risers on PTFE/fluoropolymer laminate (Df ~0.001 vs ~0.01-0.02 for FR-4 class) so two-DIMMs-per-channel topologies keep DDR5-6400 instead of derating to ~4400.
why: Capacity per socket at unchanged interface: doubles DIMM count per channel without a speed penalty, so lower-density, more available DIMMs can meet capacity targets.

title: Bookbinding spine: sidewall-plated interconnect replaces TSVs
idea: Stack thinned dies like book pages, with pads routed to and exposed on one edge. Then form a 'spine' of vertical Cu lines on the stack sidewall with a laser-patterned seed and electroless plating plus electroplating below 100 C.
why: No TSVs means no TSV keep-out, TSV yield loss or via thermal budget. HBM area per bit could move toward DDR5 levels, roughly 2x better.

title: Free-space optical memory modules on kinematic mounts
idea: MINIFY contact to none: memory modules drop into a slot with a three-ball kinematic mount, and lenses align free-space optical beams to the host, so there are no connectors to wear and modules swap tool-free.
why: Off-package memory at ~1-2 pJ/bit with field-replaceable, reusable modules; frees interposer area.

title: Active glass interposer with oxide-TFT repeaters
idea: Move the PHY into the substrate: build low-temperature IGZO thin-film-transistor repeaters, multiplexers and charge-recycling drivers directly on a glass interposer (sputter plus contact litho, <350 C), so memory and compute dies use tiny low-swing pads and the interposer regenerates signals over centimetres.
why: Fact 7: strips much PHY area from DRAM dies, and memory can sit further from compute for more capacity at ~0.5 pJ/bit; TFT-on-glass is a university process.

title: IKEA flat-pack: onshore U.S. assembly of imported known-good DRAM
idea: Flat-pack furniture ships compact and is put together near the buyer. Import thinned, tested DRAM wafers, then do all stacking, ≤300 C hybrid bonding, base-die attach and packaging in U.S. brownfield sites whose tools all run ≤400 C.
why: Packaging capex is ~10x lower than a DRAM fab and can be online in 1-2 years. It brings HBM value-add and supply-chain control onshore before front-end fabs exist.

title: Origami: one folded thinned DRAM strip forms an 8-high stack
idea: Forced 'origami': instead of dicing and stacking 8 dies, a strip of 8 adjacent DRAM dies is left joined, thinned, and coated with polyimide redistribution that runs across flexible hinge zones; the strip is then folded accordion-style into a stack. Tiers connect through the hinges, so there are no TSVs and no die-to-die alignment.
why: HBM TSV tax and stacking yield; uses wafer-level RDL instead of TSV etch/fill and hybrid bonding tools, so capital intensity is lower.

title: Double-stack railcars: memory stacks on both interposer faces
idea: Double-stack container trains double what a track can carry. Mount HBM stacks on both the top and bottom faces of a thin interposer. Dense through-interposer vias link the underside stacks to the compute die's PHY edge, and a two-sided cold-plate sandwich cools them.
why: HBM count is capped by the compute die's shoreline. Using both faces puts ~2x the stacks within the same wire reach, so capacity per accelerator roughly doubles without longer links.

title: Active mature-node interposer packed with SRAM becomes the L4
idea: Worsen: waste a 2,500 mm^2 silicon interposer as passive copper. Flip: make the interposer an active 28-16 nm die from U.S. mature fabs, filled with SRAM banks under the routing, so the passive area becomes ~1-2 GB of latch-based buffer between HBM and logic.
why: Data movement and DRAM demand: hot working sets served at ~0.2 pJ/bit, cutting HBM traffic 30-50% with no capacitor and no EUV.

title: Disk-drive head wafer fabs pattern fine-pitch memory interposers
idea: Invert 'interposers must come from semiconductor foundries': repurpose recording-head wafer fabs in Minnesota, which already pattern sub-100 nm thin-film features, to make redistribution layers and fine-pitch interposers for memory stacks.
why: Taps idle U.S. thin-film lithography outside the congested CoWoS chain; relief for HBM integration with near-zero new fab capital.

title: LCD panel fab repurposed to print glass memory interposers
idea: Run 2 um redistribution layers on Gen-8.5 display lines (2.2 x 2.5 m glass, i-line steppers built for TFTs), the way TV panels are made, and dice them into memory interposers. No EUV and no silicon wafer is involved.
why: Huge idle display capacity yields interposer area at ~10x lower cost per mm2, relieving the 2.5D bottleneck that throttles HBM supply.

title: Array-only DRAM wafers bonded to one shared logic periphery tier
idea: Combine CMOS-bonded-array (Xtacking-style 3D NAND) with multi-tier DRAM: fabricate array-only wafers with no sense amps or decoders, then bond 2-4 of them through vertical bitline/wordline vias at ~2 um hybrid-bond pitch onto a single advanced-logic wafer carrying all sense amps, decoders and I/O.
why: Periphery (~49% of die) and masks: array wafers need fewer masks and cheap transistors while periphery gets fast logic; claims 30-45% lower cost/bit and 1.6-2x bits per footprint.

title: Sell DRAM as bondable wafers and let customers stack
idea: Reverse the HBM value chain: memory makers sell finished DRAM wafers with a published hybrid-bond pad standard, and foundries, OSATs and accelerator firms do the thinning, stacking and base-die integration themselves, creating many parallel HBM assembly lines.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: the HBM bottleneck moves from three memory makers' packaging lines to any advanced packager, including U.S. OSATs.

title: Gasless copper self-sputtering seeds high-aspect TSVs without argon
idea: Combine HiPIMS with sustained self-sputtering: above a threshold target power density ionized Cu atoms sustain the discharge on their own, so after brief ignition with N2 or H2 the process runs on copper vapor only, and the highly ionized flux is steered by substrate bias deep into 10:1 TSVs for conformal seeds.
why: Argon removal plus better step coverage: narrower TSVs and smaller keep-out zones shrink the HBM area tax.
